YesWiki BazarImportAction object-injection exploit request (CVE-2026-52777) AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound POST requests to the YesWiki BazaR importer endpoint (?BazaR&vue=importer) that carry the vulnerable importfiche parameter, the exact request shape an attacker uses to reach the unserialize() sink in CSVManager.php. Article-specific because it keys on YesWiki's own routing string rather than a generic deserialization pattern. Rationale: Uses YesWiki's exact routing tokens BazaR + vue=importer (from BazarAction::run VOIR_IMPORTER -> callAction('bazarimport')) plus POST method, which is the only path that reaches CSVManager::importEntry. Cross-checked GitLab advisory and YesWiki issue #356. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/yeswiki/yeswiki/CVE-2026-52777/ • https://github.com/YesWiki/yeswiki/issues/356
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin using the Bazar CSV import UI to import entries
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nuclei/Burp) probing the importer endpoint
  • Security team validating the CVE-2026-52777 patch on 4.6.6
  • Automated content-migration scripts that POST to the importer
  • Uptime/synthetic monitors that replay a saved import request
Suppression filter
| where csUserAgent !has "Nuclei" and csUserAgent !has "Burp" and cIP !in ("<known-scanner-ips>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request for the matched cIP/csUserName; confirm request body contained importfiche[] and whether the source is an internal admin workstation or an external/unknown IP, and check the Referer for a cross-site origin (CSRF). 2) Contain: if body carried a base64 blob or the source is untrusted, block the source IP at the WAF and force-logout/rotate the admin session; verify the host is on YesWiki >=4.6.6. 3) Hunt: search same host for php-fpm/apache spawning shells and for wakka.config.php or *.php writes under the webroot in the following 30 minutes.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriQuery has "BazaR" and csUriQuery has "vue=importer"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserName, scStatus, csUserAgent
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Base64 PHP-serialized-object payload in importfiche POST body AIExploitation High
Detects the deserialization payload itself: a request to a YesWiki host whose body contains the importfiche parameter alongside a base64 string that decodes to a PHP serialized object (prefixes Tzo = 'O:' object, YToxOnt = 'a:1:{' array as in the PoC). This is the highest-fidelity signal that an actual object-injection payload (e.g. a PHPGGC Doctrine chain) was sent, not just endpoint probing. Rationale: Combines the article's exact sink-feeding param name (importfiche, from BazarImportAction formatArguments) with base64 markers of PHP serialization grammar (Tzo/YToxOnt) exercised by base64_decode+unserialize; the PoC payload itself begins YToxOnt. Requires a WAF that logs the POST body, noted as a deployment prerequisite. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/yeswiki/yeswiki/CVE-2026-52777/ • https://github.com/ambionics/phpggc
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Bazar CSV import if any tenant still uses the legacy base64+serialize transport
  • Security researcher submitting benign serialized test objects
  • Pen-test / red-team validating CVE-2026-52777 with PHPGGC
  • WAF replaying a captured malicious request during tuning
Response runbook
1) Triage: base64-decode the matched importfiche value; if it decodes to O:<n>:"<Class>" confirm the class (e.g. Doctrine\*) and whether it is a known PHPGGC gadget. 2) Contain: block the source at the WAF, isolate the YesWiki host pending review, and rotate the targeted admin session/credentials; patch to >=4.6.6. 3) Hunt: on the host, look for php-fpm/apache child shells, new webshells under the webroot, and outbound connections initiated by the web-server user in the minutes after the request.

YesWiki web-server process spawning an OS shell (deserialization RCE outcome) AIExploitation High
Detects the payoff of a successful PHPGGC Doctrine/RCE1 chain: the YesWiki web-server process (php-fpm/apache2/httpd/nginx) spawning a shell or download/exec utility. On a normal YesWiki host these processes never fork /bin/sh, curl, wget or python. Rationale: The article states Doctrine/RCE1 terminates in system($cmd); the observable is the web-server process forking a shell/downloader, which on a PHP wiki host is essentially never benign. Parent set (php-fpm/apache2/httpd/nginx) is article/stack-specific. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/yeswiki/yeswiki/CVE-2026-52777/ • https://github.com/ambionics/phpggc
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A YesWiki plugin/cron legitimately shelling out via exec() (e.g. image conversion via ImageMagick/convert)
  • Deployment or backup scripts run under the web-server user
  • Composer/npm build steps executed by the web account during updates
  • Health-check scripts invoking curl from the app tier
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "ImageMagick" and ProcessCommandLine !has "/usr/bin/convert" and not (FileName in~ ("curl","wget") and ProcessCommandLine has "healthcheck")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child command line and the php-fpm parent; determine if it maps to a known plugin/cron or is an ad-hoc shell (id/whoami/reverse-shell). 2) Contain: kill the process tree, isolate the host, and preserve the php-fpm worker for forensics; block any C2 IP seen. 3) Hunt: enumerate files written by the web-server user (webshells, wakka.config.php), review MySQL access, and pivot to other sites on the same shared host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-fpm","php-fpm7.4","php-fpm8.1","php-fpm8.2","httpd","apache2","nginx","php")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","ksh","curl","wget","python","python3","perl","nc","ncat")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| sort by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","httpd","apache2","nginx")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/curl","/wget","/python","/perl","/nc")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

YesWiki wakka.config.php modified by web-server account (post-RCE persistence) AIInstallation High
Alerts when YesWiki's core config file wakka.config.php is created/modified by a web-server process (php-fpm/apache/nginx). The advisory names wakka.config.php as an explicit post-exploitation target; that file is not rewritten by the web tier during normal operation, so a web-server-initiated write is a strong persistence/tamper signal. Rationale: Advisory Impact section explicitly lists modifying wakka.config.php as an attacker post-exploitation action; the file+web-process-initiator pairing is high-fidelity because the web tier does not rewrite core config in normal use. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/yeswiki/yeswiki/CVE-2026-52777/
ATT&CKT1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin running the YesWiki installer/updater under the web-server user which rewrites wakka.config.php
  • A legitimate config-change action performed through the wiki admin UI
  • Automated provisioning/IaC re-templating the config file
  • Migration to 4.6.6 that touches the config during upgrade
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "install" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "update" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "upgrade"
Response runbook
1) Triage: diff the new wakka.config.php against the last known-good version; check for injected PHP, altered DB creds, or debug/eval flags, and correlate with an importfiche POST in the prior 30 min. 2) Contain: restore the vetted config, isolate the host, and rotate DB and admin credentials; upgrade to >=4.6.6. 3) Hunt: scan the webroot for newly written *.php (webshells), review recent web-server-spawned processes, and inspect MySQL for unauthorized dumps.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "wakka.config.php"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("php-fpm","httpd","apache2","nginx","php")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| sort by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName has "wakka.config.php"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","httpd","apache2","nginx","php")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, EventType
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

YesWiki unauthenticated erasespamedcomments page-deletion invocation (CVE-2026-52766) AIExploitation High
Hunts POST requests to a YesWiki instance that reference the `erasespamedcomments` action together with the `clean`/`suppr[]` deletion parameters, the exact request shape from the CVE-2026-52766 PoC. Because the action performs no authorization or CSRF check, any single such request from an unauthenticated source is a live exploitation attempt for arbitrary wiki page deletion (including PagePrincipale). Rationale: Uses the CVE-specific action name `erasespamedcomments` plus the `suppr[]`/`clean=yes` deletion parameters from the advisory PoC (POST /?wiki=SpamCleanup, clean=yes&suppr[0]=...). The action name is unique to YesWiki and the parameter trio is otherwise never seen, giving a near-zero-FP signature; requires a log source that captures POST body/full query (WAF or app log) since IIS alone omits the body. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6x7x-gcmf-7r8x • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-52766
ATT&CKT1190 T1485
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authenticated wiki admin legitimately running spam-comment cleanup after a spam wave
  • Security scanner / DAST tool (Burp, Nuclei) firing a CVE-2026-52766 test request in an authorized pentest
  • Vulnerability-management team validating the patch on a staging YesWiki host
  • A WAF replay/allow-list health check that reissues a captured deletion request
Suppression filter
| where csUserName == "" or isempty(csUserName)   // keep only unauthenticated callers; authenticated admin cleanup is expected
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request for the matching cIP/src — confirm it is unauthenticated (empty csUserName) and enumerate the tags inside suppr[]; check whether PagePrincipale or admin pages are named. 2) Contain: if unauthenticated and unexpected, block the source IP at the WAF, put the YesWiki instance into hibernation (WIKI_IN_HIBERNATION) or take it offline, and confirm the app is upgraded to >=4.6.6. 3) Hunt: search all access logs from the same src for the preceding trigger-page creation (POST to */edit carrying {{erasespamedcomments}}) and for a 404 spike on the deleted tags; restore affected pages from DB/page-history backup.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem has "erasespamedcomments" or csUriQuery has_any ("erasespamedcomments","suppr","clean=yes")
| project TimeGenerated, cIP, csMethod, sSiteName, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserName, csUserAgent, Computer
| order by TimeGenerated desc

YesWiki confirmed mass page deletion — bulk 'Suppression de la page' / deletion-request burst (CVE-2026-52766) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the impact stage of CVE-2026-52766: a burst of confirmed page deletions in a short window, either as YesWiki admin-log 'Suppression de la page' entries (application log) or as a spike of erasespamedcomments/suppr deletion POSTs from one source. Legitimate admin cleanup touches 1-3 pages; mass abuse deletes many tags in one automated run. Rationale: Pivots on the exact admin-log string `Suppression de la page` written by PageController::delete()->LogAdministrativeAction (article code), and on a per-source burst of suppr/erasespamedcomments POSTs. Volume + the CVE-specific action string separates automated mass deletion from routine single-page maintenance; the app-log path also confirms deletions actually succeeded rather than merely being attempted. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6x7x-gcmf-7r8x • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-52766
ATT&CKT1485
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Wiki admin performing a large legitimate content purge/migration (decommissioning a namespace)
  • Scripted maintenance job that deletes stale pages in bulk on a schedule
  • Restore/reimport operation that deletes-then-recreates many pages
  • Spam wave genuinely being cleaned by an authorized moderator using the intended feature
Response runbook
1) Triage: expand the make_set of SamplePages / suppr tags to see which pages were deleted and whether PagePrincipale, admin, or other users' pages are included; correlate to the source IP and whether it was authenticated. 2) Contain: hibernate or isolate the YesWiki host, block the source IP, and confirm the upgrade to >=4.6.6 (or apply an ACL gating erasespamedcomments to admins). 3) Hunt: pull page-history/DB backups and restore deleted tags; check for the initial trigger-page creation and for follow-on defacement or re-creation of the front page by the same source.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SyslogMessage has "Suppression de la page"
| summarize DeletedPages = count(), SamplePages = make_set(SyslogMessage, 50), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by HostName, ProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where DeletedPages > 5   // >5 confirmed page deletions in a 10-min window — far above manual admin cleanup (typ. 1-3)
| order by DeletedPages desc

YesWiki page-deletion aftermath — 404 spike on previously-valid wiki pages (CVE-2026-52766) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the downstream impact of CVE-2026-52766: pages deleted by the erasespamedcomments abuse now return HTTP 404 to normal visitors. A sudden spike of 404s across many distinct wiki page paths in a short window — especially minutes after an erasespamedcomments POST — indicates successful mass deletion. Rationale: Uses the YesWiki URL shape (`?wiki=<PageTag>`) plus a 404 status spike across many distinct page tags, which is the observable end state after PageManager::deleteOrphaned() wipes pages/links/acls/tags rows. Best deployed as a same-source time-window correlation with UC1's erasespamedcomments POST to cut ambiguity from ordinary broken-link 404s. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6x7x-gcmf-7r8x • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-52766
ATT&CKT1485
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Broken-link crawler / SEO bot hitting many stale URLs
  • Legitimate content restructure where pages were intentionally renamed or removed
  • A vulnerability scanner enumerating non-existent wiki page tags
  • Cache/CDN warm-up requesting pages that legitimately never existed
Suppression filter
| where csUriStem has_any ("wiki") | where DistinctPages > 10 and NotFound > 20   // require both breadth (distinct pages) and volume to suppress lone broken-link crawlers
Response runbook
1) Triage: list the distinct 404 page tags and check whether any were serving 200 in the hours before the spike (a genuine deletion signature) versus never-existed paths (scanner noise). 2) Contain: if prior-200 pages are now 404, treat as confirmed destruction — isolate the host, block the abusing source from UC1/UC2, and confirm patch >=4.6.6. 3) Hunt: correlate the 404 tags to the suppr[] array values in the preceding erasespamedcomments POST from the same window/source, then restore the affected pages from backup and monitor for re-deletion.
W3CIISLog

| where csMethod == "GET"

| summarize NotFound = count(), DistinctPages = dcount(csUriQuery), Pages = make_set(csUriQuery, 50) by Computer, sSiteName, bin(TimeGenerated, 15m)
| where DistinctPages > 10   // >10 distinct previously-served wiki pages now 404 in a 15-min window — deletion aftermath
| order by NotFound desc

Talos prevalent-malware SHA256 execution (UAT-7810 telemetry batch) AIInstallation Medium
Alerts on execution of any file matching the four SHA256 hashes listed in the Talos report's most-prevalent-malware section. Article-specific: exact hashes, so any match is a confirmed known-bad binary. Rationale: Uses the four exact SHA256 values published by Talos (VID001.exe coinminer, SECOH-QAD.exe procpatcher, etc.). These are the article's most-prevalent-malware batch; hash matches are unambiguous known-bad, though attribution to LONGLEASH/DOGLEASH is not confirmed by Talos.
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst detonating the sample in an approved sandbox VM
  • IR responder copying the sample onto a forensic host for analysis
  • EDR/AV quarantine relocation event re-hashing the file
  • Threat-intel enrichment tool staging the sample for detonation
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("malware-sandbox01","ir-forensics01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SHA256 hit, the executing user/host, and whether the host is a sanctioned analysis VM. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and quarantine the binary; block the hashes org-wide. 3) Hunt: pivot the host for outbound to the four ORB relay IPs, check autoruns/services for SECOH-QAD.exe (procpatcher) persistence, and sweep the estate for the same hashes.

Edge device recruited as ORB relay — inbound sessions from UAT-7810 IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Detects internal hosts or edge appliances ACCEPTING inbound connections from the four UAT-7810 relay IPs — the signature of a node being used as an ORB proxy conduit for secondary APT traffic, distinct from outbound beaconing. Rationale: Same four relay IPs but pivots on the INBOUND direction — matches the article's core thesis that UAT-7810 turns edge devices into relay nodes routing secondary-actor traffic; a device accepting sessions from these IPs is likely a recruited ORB node.
ATT&CKT1133 T1090.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate inbound service (VPN/remote-mgmt) that the IP was temporarily reassigned to
  • Firewall logging a blocked inbound attempt (still worth review but not a compromise)
  • Internet background-radiation scan hitting an exposed port
  • Threat-intel honeypot deliberately accepting the connection
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the connection was ACCEPTED (not blocked) and identify the listening service/port and the receiving host role. 2) Contain: ACL the four IPs inbound, isolate the device if it is not a designed remote-access endpoint, and capture the listening process. 3) Hunt: inspect the host for proxy/tunnel tooling, correlate with outbound sessions to different downstream targets (relay-through pattern), and review config for unauthorized port-forward rules.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Web

| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Transitive install of poisoned @injectivelabs 1.20.21 build under node_modules
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Compromised @injectivelabs/sdk-ts exfiltrates wallet keys through fake telemetry
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Malicious @injectivelabs SDK build artifact by SHA-256 on disk · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Exfil to lookalike Injective gRPC-web subdomain (@injectivelabs stealer C2) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Exfil to lookalike Injective gRPC-web subdomain (@injectivelabs stealer C2) AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound DNS/network activity to testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network, the character-code-rebuilt exfil host used by the trojanized @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21 to smuggle base64 wallet key material inside an X-Request-Id header disguised as gRPC-web traffic. Article-specific because the FQDN is a fixed IOC unique to this campaign. Rationale: The exfil FQDN testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network is a fixed, campaign-unique IOC (a lookalike subdomain never served by real Injective infra); matching it exactly avoids the FP risk of the parent injective.network.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1132.001 T1041 T1001.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate future Injective testnet archival endpoint being stood up under this exact FQDN (verify DNS/PKI ownership)
  • Security tooling / sandbox detonating the malicious package intentionally
  • Threat-intel sinkhole or research VM deliberately resolving the IOC
  • Internal DNS logging replaying old cached queries
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the resolving host ran an @injectivelabs-dependent app; capture the initiating process (node.exe) and user. 2) Contain: block the FQDN at DNS/proxy/firewall, isolate the host, and treat every wallet mnemonic/private key derived on it as exposed — freeze/rotate. 3) Hunt: pivot to all hosts querying the FQDN, pull package-lock/yarn.lock for @injectivelabs/*@1.20.21, and search DeviceFileEvents for the two malicious build artifacts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, DnsResponseCodeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious @injectivelabs SDK build artifact by SHA-256 on disk AIInstallation Medium
Detects the two poisoned build files (accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs / accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js) from @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21 landing on disk, matched on their exact SHA-256 hashes. High fidelity IOC match that survives file renaming. Rationale: Both SHA-256 values are published IOCs for the exact malicious build artifacts; a hash match is unambiguous and near-zero FP, catching the stealer even if the file is renamed during transitive install.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / malware analyst intentionally storing the sample
  • Backup or EDR quarantine copy of the artifact triggering a second file event
  • Threat-intel feed ingestion writing the IOC file to a sandbox share
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the writing process and host; confirm whether it is a dev/CI machine or an analyst sandbox. 2) Contain: isolate the host, remove the affected node_modules, and pin @injectivelabs/* to a clean version (>=1.20.23); treat any wallet keys handled on the host as compromised. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints/CI runners for the same hashes and for outbound contact to the exfil FQDN.

| where SHA256 in ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 in ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Transitive install of poisoned @injectivelabs 1.20.21 build under node_modules AIDelivery Medium
Structural supply-chain detection: the campaign-unique build filenames accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs / accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js appearing under a node_modules/@injectivelabs path. Resilient to re-signing/re-hash because it keys on the version-marker filenames + package scope rather than the SHA-256, catching victims who pulled the stealer transitively via any of the 18 sibling packages. Rationale: The build filenames accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs / accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js are unique to the poisoned 1.20.21 dist and act as a version marker; combined with the node_modules/@injectivelabs scope this flags transitive victims (e.g. via wallet-core) who never named sdk-ts directly, and survives re-hash of the still-downloadable deprecated package.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Aikido/other scanner replaying the artifact during a rescan
  • Developer intentionally checking out the compromised version to reproduce/analyze
  • A future clean @injectivelabs build coincidentally reusing the same hashed chunk name (unlikely — Rollup chunk hashes are content-derived)
Response runbook
1) Triage: on each hit, read the package's package.json version and lockfile to confirm 1.20.21 was resolved (directly or transitively). 2) Contain: delete node_modules, repin @injectivelabs/* to >=1.20.23, and rebuild; flag any wallet keys/seed phrases derived on the host for rotation. 3) Hunt: enumerate every repo/CI job with @injectivelabs/*@1.20.21 in lockfiles and correlate hosts against exfil-domain contacts and the SHA-256 file detection.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs", "accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js")
| where FolderPath contains "node_modules" and FolderPath contains "injectivelabs"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs", "accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js")
| where TargetFilePath contains "node_modules" and TargetFilePath contains "injectivelabs"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or SHA1 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or MD5 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or SHA1 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or MD5 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — One Target, Two Flags | Rival Espionage Actors Converge On Pakistani Law Enforce
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound C2 to PlugX/ShadowPad/Cobalt Strike/Remcos infrastructure targeting Pakistani law enforcement · [LLM] Compromised web-application server beaconing to espionage C2 (portal-update implant) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Outbound C2 to PlugX/ShadowPad/Cobalt Strike/Remcos infrastructure targeting Pakistani law enforcement AICommand & Control High
Hunts any internal host establishing outbound connections to the 13 C2 IPs SentinelLABS attributed to the four tooling clusters (PlugX, ShadowPad, Cobalt Strike, Remcos) converging on Balochistan Police and other Pakistani law-enforcement orgs between Feb 2024 and Apr 2026. Pure network-IOC match on disclosed espionage C2 servers. Rationale: Anchored on the exact 13 C2 IPs from Table 1 / code blocks (PlugX 172.111.233.x + 172.94.9.x + 45.74.6.17, ShadowPad 45.125.32.218, Cobalt Strike 142.171.183.8 + 193.42.25.65, Remcos 89.31.121.220). Any egress to these known-bad hosts is high-fidelity; the tooling families and Pakistani-entity victimology are corroborated externally, though the specific IPs are from the SentinelLABS primary report only. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/one-target-china-india-espionage-converge-on-pakistani-law-enforcement/ • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.shadowpad • https://thehackernews.com/2023/07/pakistani-entities-targeted-in.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573 T1219
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / threat-intel analyst deliberately sandboxing or sinkholing one of these IPs from a corporate host
  • IP reassignment after takedown — a benign service later hosted on a recycled VPS IP (172.94.9.x / 45.x hosting ranges are commodity VPS)
  • Internal threat-intel validation tooling or EDR connectivity checks pinging the IOC list
  • Proxy/NAT concentration causing many internal hosts to appear as one src toward the IP
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe") // exclude EDR/AV connectivity-check processes
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the connection is genuinely outbound and established (not a blocked/attempt), identify the initiating process and host role — servers hosting the CMS/FIR/HRMIS/HotelEye/CRMS apps are highest priority. 2) Contain: block all 13 IPs at perimeter, isolate the host, snapshot memory before reboot to preserve PlugX/ShadowPad in-memory implants. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for DLL side-loading (unsigned DLL next to a signed EXE), scheduled tasks/Run keys created near first-seen, and lateral SMB/RDP from the host; sweep the org for any other host touching the same /24s (172.111.233.0/24, 172.94.9.0/24).

| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), ConnCount=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort, 20) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by LastSeen desc

Compromised web-application server beaconing to espionage C2 (portal-update implant) AICommand & Control Medium
Tighter server-side pivot: a web/application-server process (IIS w3wp, Apache/Tomcat java, nginx, php-cgi) on a Pakistani law-enforcement web server initiating outbound to the disclosed C2 IPs. Grounds on the article's China-nexus 'custom implants masquerading as a portal update' planted in one of the citizen/police web applications (e.g. the Complaint Management System). Rationale: Combines the exact C2 IP set with a server-process filter to isolate the article's specific scenario — a China-nexus implant planted in a citizen/police web application (CMS) beaconing out. Web-server processes reaching commodity-VPS C2 IPs is extremely rare and high-fidelity, and directly targets the compromised-webapp vector the article calls out. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/one-target-china-india-espionage-converge-on-pakistani-law-enforcement/ • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.shadowpad
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1505.003 T1573
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Web app legitimately calling an outbound API that happens to be on a recycled VPS IP after IOC takedown
  • Java-based agent/monitoring on the web server making outbound telemetry calls
  • Server-side update/package fetch (Tomcat/Maven, php composer) to a mirror on the same hosting range
  • App-server health-check or CDN origin-pull to a reassigned address
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "maven" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "composer" // exclude server package-manager fetches
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which web application the process serves (CMS/FIR/HRMIS/AVLS/HotelEye/CRMS) and whether the beacon started after a recent 'portal update'/deployment window; review web-root for recently modified/added handler, JSP, ASPX or PHP files. 2) Contain: take the web app offline or block egress, preserve IIS/Tomcat logs and web-root for forensics, rotate app/service and DB credentials the server can reach. 3) Hunt: search web access logs (W3CIISLog/AppServiceHTTPLogs) for the implant's request pattern, look for webshell-style POSTs, and pivot to any DB export or biometric/criminal-record access from the compromised app identity.

| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where RemoteIP in (C2)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("w3wp.exe","java.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe","php-cgi.exe","tomcat.exe","javaw.exe","node.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc

Symlinks Are Still Scary (And Yes, You Can Commit Them to Git)

Snyk
2026-07-09 5 use cases 2 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

A harmless-looking symlink in a Git repo can redirect a tool into reading or writing anywhere on your machine. That old trick is now showing up in AI coding assistants, with nasty results.

CVEsCVE-2026-12958 CVE-2026-50549 CVE-2024-32002 CVE-2024-21626 CVE-2021-32803
ATT&CKT1190 T1195.002

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Git-spawned hook execution during recursive clone (CVE-2024-32002) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SSH authorized_keys written by non-SSH tooling (symlink repo payload) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Symlinks Are Still Scary (And Yes, You Can Commit Them to Git)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
SSH authorized_keys written by non-SSH tooling (symlink repo payload) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts writes/modifications to any user's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys where the writing process is NOT legitimate SSH provisioning tooling — the payoff of the article's headline attack, where a symlink named like project_settings.json checked out from a cloned repo resolves to authorized_keys and a build script/editor/AI coding agent silently writes an attacker key through it. Because the OS resolves the symlink transparently, the file event reports the real target path (.ssh/authorized_keys), which is the tell. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact payload path ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (code Block 1) written by non-SSH tooling — the symlink resolves so the OS reports the real target, making the write-through observable. Cross-checked MITRE T1098.004, Splunk Security Content and Elastic authorized_keys rules to confirm the technique and avoid duplicating a generic FIM rule by scoping on the writing process. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/004/ • https://research.splunk.com/endpoint/f5ab595e-28e5-4327-8077-5008ba97c850/ • https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/security/prebuilt-rules/rules/cross-platform/persistence_ssh_authorized_keys_modification
ATT&CKT1098.004 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Ansible/Puppet/Salt/Terraform pushing authorized_keys via a config-management run (excluded, but custom wrappers may slip through)
  • Developer legitimately running ssh-copy-id or manually editing authorized_keys with vim/nano
  • Cloud-init / provisioning agent seeding keys on first boot of a new VM
  • CI runner injecting a deploy key into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys as an intended step
  • Dotfile-management tools (chezmoi, GNU stow) that symlink or template SSH config
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("terraform","authorized_keys_command","chezmoi","stow") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "ansible"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcess chain — is the writer a dev tool (git, node, python, code, cursor) or shell spawned from a freshly cloned repo path? Compare the written key fingerprint against the user's known keys and check if the file is/was a symlink (ls -l ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, readlink). 2) Contain: if the key is unrecognized, remove the offending authorized_keys line, kill active sessions authenticated by it, and rotate the account; quarantine the source repo. 3) Hunt: search the same host/user for the source symlink (git ls-files -s | grep '^120000'), other writes to ~/.ssh, ~/.bashrc, ~/.git/hooks, and any inbound SSH logons using the added key.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FolderPath endswith "/.ssh/authorized_keys" or (FileName == "authorized_keys" and FolderPath has "/.ssh")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sshd","ssh","ssh-keygen","ssh-copy-id","cloud-init","useradd","adduser","ansible","puppet","chef-client","salt-minion")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetFilePath endswith "/.ssh/authorized_keys" or (TargetFileName == "authorized_keys" and TargetFilePath has "/.ssh")
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRename")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("sshd","ssh-keygen","ssh-copy-id","cloud-init","ansible","puppet","salt-minion"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SSH authorized_keys Written by Non-SSH Tooling (Symlink Repo Payload)
id: 5c2e6b1a-9f3d-4a77-8b0e-2d1c6f9a4e21
description: Detects creation or modification of a user's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys by a process that is not legitimate SSH provisioning tooling, consistent with a symlink committed to a cloned git repository resolving to authorized_keys and being written through by a build script, editor, or AI coding agent.
references:
  - https://snyk.io/blog/symlinks-are-still-scary/
  - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/004/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/10
tags:
  - attack.t1098.004
  - attack.persistence
logsource:
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|endswith: '/.ssh/authorized_keys'
  filter_legit:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/sshd'
      - '/ssh-keygen'
      - '/ssh-copy-id'
      - '/cloud-init'
      - '/ansible'
      - '/salt-minion'
  condition: selection and not filter_legit
level: medium
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.command_line:(*authorized_keys* AND (*">>"* OR *tee* OR *">"*)) -@process.executable.path:(*/sshd OR */ssh-keygen OR */ssh-copy-id OR */cloud-init)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\/\.ssh\/authorized_keys$/i
| NOT (ContextImageFileName=/\/(sshd|ssh-keygen|ssh-copy-id|cloud-init)$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_path="*/.ssh/authorized_keys" Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified","renamed") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action Filesystem.process_guid
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

Git-spawned hook execution during recursive clone (CVE-2024-32002) AIExploitation High
Hunts a process whose image lives inside a .git/hooks/ directory and whose parent is git — the exact signature of CVE-2024-32002, where a malicious repository's crafted submodule + symlink writes a hook into .git/ that git executes while the clone is still running, yielding RCE from nothing more than git clone --recurse-submodules. No build step or 'run the project' required. Rationale: Anchored on the CVE-2024-32002 mechanic named in the article (git clone --recurse-submodules dropping a script into .git/hooks and running it during clone). The parent=git + child-image-in-.git/hooks pair is high-fidelity because hooks are not supposed to execute during a clone; confirmed via the git security advisory GHSA-8h77-4q3w-gfgv and Amal Murali's PoC writeup. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/git/git/security/advisories/GHSA-8h77-4q3w-gfgv • https://amalmurali.me/posts/git-rce/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2024/05/16/git-cve-2024-32002/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer with legitimately installed local git hooks (post-checkout/post-merge) firing during a normal pull or checkout
  • Husky / pre-commit framework hooks that shell out during commit or checkout operations
  • CI systems that intentionally invoke repo hooks as part of a pipeline stage
  • git-lfs post-checkout smudge hooks running on a large-file repo clone
  • Monorepo tooling (e.g. Nx, Turborepo) that registers checkout hooks
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("husky","git-lfs","post-merge") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pull","checkout HEAD","lfs"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the executed hook file under .git/hooks/ and the InitiatingProcessCommandLine — confirm it was a clone/--recurse-submodules op and read the hook body for network callbacks or key writes. Check git version on host against the patched set (>=2.39.4/2.40.2/2.41.1/2.42.2/2.43.4/2.44.1/2.45.1). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the hook process tree, and quarantine the cloned repo directory; block the source repo URL. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for downstream child processes of the hook, writes to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, new persistence (cron, systemd units, shell rc files), and outbound C2 from the hook's PID.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FolderPath has_any ("/.git/hooks/", "\\.git\\hooks\\")

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Joro proxy-mode confused-deputy: browser POSTs to loopback API 127.0.0.1:9090 (CVE-2026-53649)

Joro proxy-mode confused-deputy: browser POSTs to loopback API 127.0.0.1:9090 (CVE-2026-53649) AIDelivery Low
Hunts a web browser process opening connections to the Joro proxy-mode API on loopback TCP/9090, the confused-deputy vector CVE-2026-53649 abuses when attacker-controlled cross-origin JavaScript reaches the unauthenticated, wildcard-CORS Joro API. Article-specific because it pins the exact bind (127.0.0.1:9090) and the browser-mediated initiator. Rationale: Uses the exact loopback bind (127.0.0.1:9090) named in the advisory plus a browser-process initiator, the confused-deputy shape of CVE-2026-53649. Deliberately hunting/Low because a legitimate Joro operator's own browser talks to the same UI/API port. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqhv-chqm-fhcc • https://bishopfox.com/blog/introducing-joro-using-ai-build-security-tooling • https://github.com/bishopfox
ATT&CKT1189 T1204.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Joro operator using the proxy-mode web UI, which itself talks to 127.0.0.1:9090
  • Unrelated local dev services on 9090 (Prometheus Pushgateway, SonarQube, custom app) that a browser hits
  • Browser DevTools/extension polling a localhost dev server on the same port
  • Local reverse-proxy or API mock bound to 9090 during development
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether Joro is installed/running on the host and whether the operator was actively using the Joro UI at that timestamp; pull the browser history for the immediately preceding external navigation. 2) Contain: if the loopback hit was NOT operator-initiated UI use, kill the joro process, isolate the host, and block the external page's domain at the proxy. 3) Hunt: pivot to whether joro subsequently wrote a .so plugin, restarted, or spawned an interactive shell (see companion UCs) — that sequence confirms exploitation.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 9090
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("firefox","firefox-bin","chrome","chromium","msedge","brave","Google Chrome","Firefox")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalIP
| order by Timestamp desc

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Joro native plugin RCE: joro process spawns interactive /bin/bash shell (CVE-2026-53649) AIExploitation High
Alerts when the joro binary spawns an interactive Unix shell (bash/sh/dash/zsh with -i), the terminal step of the CVE-2026-53649 chain where a malicious uploaded plugin's init() opens a goroutine and yields an interactive /bin/bash -i shell as the operator's user. High fidelity because joro is a proxy/teamserver, not a shell launcher — it has no legitimate reason to fork a local login shell. Rationale: Pins the article's exact parent (joro) and payload (interactive /bin/bash -i obtained on plugin.Open() init()). Because Joro is a proxy that never legitimately forks a local login shell, parent=joro + shell + -i is a near-zero-FP RCE tell. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqhv-chqm-fhcc • https://bishopfox.com/blog/introducing-joro-using-ai-build-security-tooling
ATT&CKT1203 T1059.004 T1129
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Joro developer/operator debugging the tool and manually shelling out from a plugin during testing
  • A local wrapper or helper script also named 'joro' that legitimately invokes a shell
  • Operator running a benign self-authored plugin that spawns a shell for tooling
  • CI/build harness building Joro plugins that exec a shell as part of a test
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "--build-plugin" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--build-plugin"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child shell's full process tree and any sockets it holds (ss -p); confirm the joro process previously loaded a newly-written .so and restarted. 2) Contain: kill the shell and joro process, isolate the host, and snapshot /proc for the joro PID before termination for the loaded-plugin path. 3) Hunt: enumerate the Joro plugin directory for attacker-uploaded .so files, review recent POSTs to /api/v1/plugins/upload and /api/v1/system/restart, and check outbound connections from joro to external hosts.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "joro"
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","ash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-i"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "joro"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","ash")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "-i"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Joro writes a native .so plugin: attacker plugin drop before restart (CVE-2026-53649) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the joro process writing a shared-object (.so) plugin file to disk, the staging step where CVE-2026-53649's unauthenticated upload endpoint persists an attacker-supplied native plugin that executes its init() on the next plugin.Open(). Article-specific via the joro-process writer plus the .so plugin artifact. Rationale: Ties the article's plugin-upload artifact (a native .so consumed by plugin.Open()) to the joro process as writer. joro dropping a .so it did not build interactively is the on-disk footprint of the upload endpoint being abused. Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator legitimately installing/updating a Joro plugin through the intended workflow

Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the written .so, submit to sandbox/AV, and check whether it was preceded by a browser hit to 127.0.0.1:9090 and a joro restart. 2) Contain: quarantine the .so, stop joro before it re-opens the plugin, and isolate the host if the file is unsigned/unknown. 3) Hunt: look for joro spawning an interactive shell or making outbound public connections after the write, and sweep other operator hosts for the same .so hash (one ABI-matched plugin works against every operator on the release).

| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

Nuclio CronJob container args carry injected shell (CVE-2026-52831 header/body OS command injection) AIExploitation High
Hunts Kubernetes API audit events that create/update a CronJob whose container args are the Nuclio '/bin/sh -c curl ...' string but also contain shell metacharacters or a service-account-token read — the signature of CVE-2026-52831 header-key/body command injection. Nuclio's legitimate cron CronJob is a pure curl invocation, so any command substitution or ';' break inside those args is exploitation. Rationale: Uses the article's exact injection sink: CronJob container args = '/bin/sh -c curl --silent --header ...' (lazy.go:2212). A benign Nuclio cron job is a pure curl, so command-substitution ('$('), a ';'-broken header, '&&', backticks, or a serviceaccount/token read inside those args is unambiguous CVE-2026-52831 exploitation. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v5px-423j-pf7p • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/nuclio/nuclio/CVE-2026-52831/ • https://corgea.com/advisories/packages/go/github.com/nuclio/nuclio
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Nuclio operator legitimately sets a curl '--data' body that happens to contain a literal '$(' as text (rare, but possible in templated payloads)
  • An admin manually editing a CronJob to add a debug '&& echo' step during troubleshooting
  • Third-party K8s tooling that wraps curl health-checks in '/bin/sh -c' with chained commands in the same namespace
  • A custom (non-Nuclio) CronJob that legitimately reads the service-account token and pipes it to curl for an in-cluster API call
Suppression filter
| where not (ReqStr has "nuclio.io/skip-scan")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the flagged CronJob's full args from the audit RequestObject; identify the injected command after the header break or inside '$()'. Trace back to the NuclioFunction trigger spec (event.headers key / event.body) that seeded it and the user/service-account that applied it. 2) Contain: 'kubectl delete cronjob <name> -n <namespace>' immediately (it has NO ownerReferences so it will NOT cascade-delete), suspend the parent NuclioFunction, and rotate the pod's service-account token if the injected command read it. 3) Hunt: enumerate all CronJobs in the nuclio namespace for the same markers, review kube-apiserver audit for other create/patch calls from the same actor, and check egress from cron pods to unexpected hosts.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| where tostring(ObjectRef.resource) == "cronjobs"
| where Stage == "ResponseComplete"
| extend ReqStr = tostring(RequestObject)
| where ReqStr has "/bin/sh" and ReqStr has "curl"
| where ReqStr has_any ("$(", "; id", "; echo", "serviceaccount/token", "&&", "| sh", "`")
| extend Namespace = tostring(ObjectRef.namespace), CronJobName = tostring(ObjectRef.name), Actor = tostring(User.username)
| project TimeGenerated, Verb, Namespace, CronJobName, Actor, ReqStr
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:kubernetes.audit @verb:(create OR update OR patch) @objectRef.resource:cronjobs @requestObject.spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec.containers.args:*serviceaccount/token*
CLOUD
index=* (sourcetype="kube:apiserver:audit" OR sourcetype="kube_audit") verb IN (create,update,patch) objectRef.resource=cronjobs
| spath output=cargs path=requestObject.spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec.containers{}.args{}
| eval cargs=mvjoin(cargs," ")
| where match(cargs,"/bin/sh") AND match(cargs,"curl")
| where match(cargs,"\$\(") OR match(cargs,";\s*id") OR match(cargs,";\s*echo") OR match(cargs,"serviceaccount/token") OR match(cargs,"&&") OR match(cargs,"\|\s*sh") OR match(cargs,"`")
| table _time objectRef.namespace objectRef.name user.username cargs
| sort - _time
Nuclio cron pod shell reads Kubernetes service-account token (CVE-2026-52831 credential theft) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the runtime side of CVE-2026-52831: a shell process assembled from a Nuclio cron curl command ('curl --silent --header ...') that also reads /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token or contains '$()' command substitution. This is the injected payload actually executing and stealing the pod's cluster credential. Rationale: Anchors on the PoC payload strings — '/bin/sh -c curl --silent --header ...' plus the injected 'cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token' recon (article Step 6). The curl+header signature scopes to Nuclio cron pods; the token read or '$()' is the injected command running, making this high-fidelity credential-access telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v5px-423j-pf7p • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/nuclio/nuclio/CVE-2026-52831/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate Nuclio function whose curl body deliberately embeds shell-like text that survives into the command line
  • In-cluster health-check scripts that both curl an endpoint and echo the SA token for debugging
  • Security scanners / CIS benchmark tools that intentionally read the service-account token path to test exposure
  • A developer manually exec-ing into a cron pod and running a chained curl + id for troubleshooting
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "nuclio.io/debug"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full ProcessCommandLine and the host/pod; confirm the parent is a Nuclio cron container and decode any '$()' substitution to see what executed. Determine whether the SA token was actually exfiltrated (look for the token value flowing into a subsequent curl to an external host). 2) Contain: cordon/evict the pod, delete the offending CronJob and parent NuclioFunction, and immediately rotate the compromised service-account token (delete the secret / bounce the SA). 3) Hunt: review DeviceNetworkEvents/NetworkConnectIP4 from the pod for outbound C2, search for the stolen token being used against the kube-apiserver, and sweep other nuclio pods for the same shell pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "curl" and ProcessCommandLine has "--header"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token", "$(", "; id", "; echo")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "curl" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "--header"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token", "$(", "; id", "; echo")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
